SCALE: Improving Guidance-Free Visual Generation via Self-Contrastive Alignment for
Likelihood Estimation

Abstract

Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is essential for improving sample quality in visual generation, but it incurs substantial sampling overhead. Existing guidance-free approaches halve this cost by approximating the CFG with a single model inference, but their performance is bounded by the CFG and inherits its limitations. In this paper, we propose self-contrastive guidance (SCG), which contrasts the model’s prediction on real and self-generated samples to obtain a direct, model-based signal that pushes generation toward the true data manifold. Integrating SCG into the standard likelihood objective via reparameterization yields Self-Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation (SCALE), a guidance-free training framework that produces SCG-enhanced predictions in a single forward pass. Across class-conditional and text-to-image generation on diffusion and autoregressive models, SCALE consistently outperforms CFG-mimicking guidance-free baselines and improves further when combined with DPO, demonstrating that the self-contrastive signal yields gains complementary to both CFG and preference-based fine-tuning.

1 Introduction

Likelihood-based generative models, including diffusion [18, 53] and autoregressive (AR) models [48, 54], have demonstrated remarkable scalability and performance. Yet, for complex visual datasets, trained models often produce samples whose clarity falls short of the training images. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) [20] has thus become the de facto remedy. By contrasting unconditional and conditional predictions, CFG effectively enhances fidelity, but at the cost of doubled sampling cost.

To eliminate this overhead, recent guidance-free approaches approximate the CFG distribution with a single inference via teacher distillation [41], contrastive objectives [7], or direct reparametrization of the CFG objective [6]. While effective, these methods are fundamentally constrained to CFG and are bounded by its performance. Furthermore, recent analyses have clarified that CFG is not flawless. A primary challenge is that condition alignment and sample fidelity are entangled along a single guidance. Therefore, amplifying the CFG for higher fidelity over-amplifies the conditional signal. This often leads to distorted sampling trajectories [8], greatly exaggerated truncation [26], and mode dropping that collapses samples onto a narrow set of per-class templates [30] (Fig. 1a). Whether a single-model approach can move beyond these limitations, therefore, remains an open question.

A complementary line of work, information-based sampling guidance [21, 24] generalizes CFG by amplifying any salient information while avoiding a degraded reference that lacks it. While effective at targeting specific quality dimensions, these methods still incur additional sampling-time forward passes (if combined with CFG, the total cost steeply rises to three model evaluations per step) and rely on heuristic, domain-specific definitions of the salient information and the degraded reference.

In this paper, we propose self-contrastive guidance (SCG), which contrasts the model’s prediction on real and self-generated samples (Fig. 1b). This contrast yields a direct, model-based estimate of the model’s own approximation error, and extrapolating along it pushes the generation process toward the true data manifold. Unlike prior information-based guidance, SCG is domain-agnostic and is directly applicable to both diffusion and AR models as it relies only on model predictions.

By reparametrizing the SCG signal as a learnable term within the standard likelihood objective, we obtain Self-Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation (SCALE), a guidance-free training framework in which the model learns to directly produce SCG-enhanced predictions in a single forward pass. For conditional generation, we further integrate CFG into SCALE so that the trained model directly refines the CFG distribution rather than simply mimicking it.

Experimental results show that SCALE consistently surpasses existing guidance-free methods that only approximate CFG across diffusion and AR architectures, on both class-conditional ImageNet (DiT [44], LlamaGen [54]) and text-to-image generation (Stable Diffusion v1.5 [49]). It matches DPO-finetuned guidance-free models alone, and applying DPO on top of SCALE brings further gains (Fig. 1c). SCALE introduces minimal additional training overhead and complexity without compromising the base model’s capabilities. As a result, SCALE provides an orthogonal direction for improving guidance-free visual generation, widely applicable to both diffusion and AR models.

2 Background

2.1 Likelihood-based Generative Models in Vision

Likelihood-based generative models aim to explicitly model the data distribution p⁡(𝒙)p({\bm{x}}). In this paper, we focus on two representative model types: diffusion [18] and autoregressive (AR) [54] models.

Diffusion models [18] aim to generate continuous data, where directly maximizing likelihood is intractable. These models learn to reverse a forward noising process that incrementally adds Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\bm{\epsilon}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) to a data 𝒙{\bm{x}}. The reverse process is learned via a score-matching objective [53], where a neural network ϵθc​(𝒙t,t,c)\bm{\epsilon}^{c}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,c) with condition cc is trained to approximate the score function ∇𝒙t​log​pt​(𝒙t)\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}) through noise prediction from noisy sample 𝒙t=αt​𝒙+σt​ϵ{\bm{x}}_{t}=\alpha_{t}{\bm{x}}+\sigma_{t}\bm{\epsilon} at timestep t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]:

ℒθDM=𝔼(𝒙0,c)∼pdata,ϵ,t​[‖ϵ−ϵθc​(𝒙t,t,c)‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\theta}^{\text{DM}}=\mathbb{E}_{({\bm{x}}_{0},c)\sim p_{\text{data}},\bm{\epsilon},t}\left[||\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{\epsilon}^{c}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},t,c)||^{2}\right], (1)

where αt\alpha_{t} and σt\sigma_{t} are scheduling functions satisfying αt2+σt2=1\alpha_{t}^{2}+\sigma_{t}^{2}=1, and 𝒙T≈ϵ{\bm{x}}_{T}\approx\bm{\epsilon}, 𝒙0≈𝒙{\bm{x}}_{0}\approx{\bm{x}}. After training, the optimal noise predictor satisfies ϵθ∗​(𝒙t)=−σt​∇𝒙t​log⁡pt​(𝒙t)\bm{\epsilon}^{*}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})=-\sigma_{t}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}), where ptp_{t} denotes the marginal distribution at step tt, enabling data generation via progressive denoising from t=Tt=T to 00.

Autoregressive models [58, 59] learn the joint distribution p⁡(𝐱,c)=∏i=1Npc​(𝒙i|𝒙<i,c),p({\mathbf{x}},c)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}p^{c}({\bm{x}}_{i}|{\bm{x}}_{<i},c), where 𝐱=(𝒙1,…,𝒙N){\mathbf{x}}=({\bm{x}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{x}}_{N}) is a discrete token sequence (e.g., vector-quantized image patches [48]) and 𝒙<i{\bm{x}}_{<i} denotes all tokens preceding 𝒙i{\bm{x}}_{i}. AR models are trained by minimizing the cross-entropy loss:

ℒθAR=𝔼(𝐱,c)∼pdata[−∑i=1Nlogpθc(𝒙i|𝒙<i,c)].\mathcal{L}_{\theta}^{\text{AR}}=\mathbb{E}_{({\mathbf{x}},c)\sim p_{\text{data}}}\left[-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p^{c}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{i}|{\bm{x}}_{<i},c)\right]. (2)

Classifier-free guidance.

For complex visual datasets, finite-capacity networks often produce samples whose clarity falls short of the training images due to approximation errors. To mitigate this gap, likelihood-based visual generative models, including diffusion and AR models, commonly employ classifier-free guidance (CFG) [11, 20, 3], which amplifies the conditional signal by extrapolating between the unconditional prediction fθuf^{u}_{\theta} and the conditional prediction fθcf^{c}_{\theta} with scale scfgs_{\text{cfg}}:

fθcfg​(𝒙t,c)=fθc​(𝒙t,c)+scfg​(fθc​(𝒙t,c)−fθu​(𝒙t)).f_{\theta}^{\text{cfg}}({\bm{x}}_{t},c)=f_{\theta}^{c}({\bm{x}}_{t},c)+s_{\text{cfg}}\ (f_{\theta}^{c}({\bm{x}}_{t},c)-f_{\theta}^{u}({\bm{x}}_{t})). (3)

For a unified formulation, we let 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t} denote the model input at step tt: the noised sample in diffusion models, or the preceding token sequence 𝒙<t{\bm{x}}_{<t} in AR models.11 1 We slightly abuse the notation tt to represent both inputs; tt denotes the timestep in diffusion, or the token index in AR. Accordingly, fθf_{\theta} is a parameterized network that serves as the noise predictor or the next-token predictor, respectively. Likewise, ptp_{t} denotes the marginal at noise level tt in diffusion and the next-token distribution given 𝒙<t{\bm{x}}_{<t} in AR.

2.2 Guidance-Free Visual Generation via Mimicking CFG

Several approaches approximate the CFG distribution ptcfgp_{t}^{\text{cfg}} with a single inference, including guidance distillation [41] for diffusion models, Condition Contrastive Alignment (CCA) [7] for AR models, and Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [6] for both. GFT in particular integrates the CFG output directly into standard likelihood training by introducing a pseudo-temperature β≔1/(1+scfg)\beta\coloneqq 1/(1+s_{\text{cfg}}) and reformulating the conditional output fθcf_{\theta}^{c} in Eq. (3) as an interpolation of CFG and unconditional predictions:

fθc​(𝒙t,c,β)=β​fθcfg​(𝒙t,c,β)+(1−β)​sg​[fθu​(𝒙t|∅,1)],\begin{split}f^{c}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},c,\beta)=\beta f^{\text{cfg}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},c,\beta)+(1-\beta)\text{sg}\left[f^{u}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}|\varnothing,1)\right],\end{split} (4)

where a stop-gradient 𝐬𝐠⁡[⋅]\mathbf{sg}[\cdot] is applied to keep the training cost minimal without affecting convergence.

Despite halving the inference cost of CFG, these methods remain constrained to the CFG-induced distribution ptcfgp_{t}^{\text{cfg}} as their training target, which alone is insufficient for high-quality generation due to its inherent limitations. In the following section, we examine these limitations and motivate a complementary guidance signal that directly improves the guidance-free visual generation.

3 Revisiting Information-Based Guidance for Guidance-Free Training

CFG is not flawless.

CFG enhances conditional generation by implicitly amplifying the conditional density to a power greater than one, sharpening the distribution toward its modes [2]. While effective, recent analyses have clarified that CFG does not merely trade compute for quality: its unconditional-to-conditional extrapolation fundamentally entangles prompt alignment and perceptual quality, making them difficult to control independently [26]. Consequently, scaling up CFG for higher fidelity disproportionately amplifies the conditional signal, driving samples off the data manifold and truncating the distribution toward a narrow set of per-class “templates” [30, 8]. Existing guidance-free generation methods halve the inference cost of CFG, but they do not address this underlying distortion. We illustrate this in Fig. 2. CFG-mimicking guidance-free methods over-amplify the conditioning signal, pulling samples away from class boundaries and off the data manifold (Fig. 2c and 2d).

Generalized Information-Based Guidance.

To address these limitations, we first revisit a complementary line of work, information-based guidance [21, 24]. It generalizes CFG by steering the sampling toward amplifying any salient information hth_{t} while avoiding degraded input samples 𝒙¯t\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t} lacking it. For diffusion models, this is formulated as

ϵ^θ​(𝒙¯t,ht)=ϵθ​(𝒙¯t,ht)+s⁡(ϵθ​(𝒙¯t,ht)−ϵθ​(𝒙¯t)),\hat{\bm{\epsilon}}_{\theta}(\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t},h_{t})=\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t},h_{t})+s\ (\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t},h_{t})-\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t})), (5)

and extends to discrete generative models from the optimization perspective22 2 While Hur et al. [24] formulate this with pθ​(𝒙~t|ht)p_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}|h_{t}), we instead use the joint pθ​(𝒙~t,ht)p_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t}). See Appendix A for details.:

arg​max𝐱¯t⁡[log⁡pθ​(𝐱¯t,ht)+s⁡(log⁡pθ​(𝐱¯t,ht)−log⁡pθ​(𝐱¯t))],\argmax_{\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}}[\log p_{\theta}(\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t},h_{t})+s\ (\log p_{\theta}(\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t},h_{t})-\log p_{\theta}(\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t}))], (6)

where ss is a guidance scale. Both formulations play the same role of amplifying hth_{t} throughout the sampling process: Eq. (5) minimizes the gradient of an implicit regressor ∇𝒙¯t​log​pim​(ht|𝒙¯t)\nabla_{\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{\text{im}}(h_{t}|\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t}) in the continuous score domain, whereas Eq. (6) directly amplifies the probability density log⁡pθ​(ht|𝒙¯t)\log p_{\theta}(h_{t}|\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t}). While these methods can target specific quality dimensions, they require additional sampling-time forward passes, and the total cost rises to three model evaluations per step if combined with CFG. Furthermore, they rely on heuristic and domain-specific choices for defining 𝒙¯t\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t} and hth_{t}, such as applying a Gaussian blur with attention mask [21] or utilizing models trained on auxiliary tasks [24].

Our approach.

Our key idea is to contrast the model’s prediction on a real sample with its prediction on a self-generated sample. This contrast provides a direct model-based signal of the discrepancy between real and self-generated samples, and pushing generation along this direction encourages samples to move toward the data manifold. Because this signal depends on real samples, it is not available at sampling time, but it arises naturally during training. We therefore incorporate it into the guidance-free training objective so that the model learns to approximate the same guidance effect with a single forward pass at inference time (Fig. 2e). Furthermore, since this formulation relies only on comparing model outputs, it applies broadly across likelihood-based generative models. In this paper, we specifically focus on two representative model types: diffusion and AR architecture.

4 Self-Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation

In this section, we formalize self-contrastive guidance (SCG) and integrate it into a guidance-free training objective, named Self-Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation (SCALE).

4.1 Self-Contrastive Guidance

We formulate SCG by contrasting outputs from real and self-generated samples. Formally, we define this by substituting a pair of real and generated samples (𝒙t,𝒙~t)({\bm{x}}_{t},\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}) into Eqs. (5) and (6), by setting 𝒙¯t=𝒙~t\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t}=\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} and ht=𝒙t−𝒙~th_{t}={\bm{x}}_{t}-\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} and assuming fθ​(𝒙~t,𝒙t−𝒙~t)=fθ​(𝒙t)f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t},{\bm{x}}_{t}-\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})=f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}):

fθscg(𝒙t)=fθ(𝒙t)+sscg(fθ(𝒙t)−fθ(𝒙~t)),f^{\text{scg}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})=f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})+s_{\text{scg}}\bigr(f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})-f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})\bigr), (7)

where sscgs_{\text{scg}} controls the strength of the SCG. This formulation applies to a broad class of generative models, including both continuous and discrete modalities. By the definition of information-based guidance above, Eq. (7) steers the sampling trajectory toward enhancing ht=𝒙t−𝒙~th_{t}={\bm{x}}_{t}-\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}, locally amplifying the model’s residual contrast between real and self-generated supports. This residual encodes how the model’s prediction on a real sample diverges from its prediction on the self-generated sample, and extrapolating along it pushes the generation toward the high-density region of the data.

4.2 Guidance-Free Training with Self-Contrastive Guidance

We integrate SCG into maximum likelihood training, so that the trained model directly approximates the self-contrastive signal and performs guidance-free sampling at sampling time. Inspired by recent guidance-free training methods [6], we reparameterize the model output fθ​(𝒙t)f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}) as an interpolation between the target SCG output fθscg​(𝒙t)f_{\theta}^{\text{scg}}({\bm{x}}_{t}) and the prediction from the self-generated sample fθ​(𝒙~t)f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}):

fθ​(𝒙t)=11+sscg​fθscg​(𝒙t)+sscg1+sscg​fθ​(𝒙~t).f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})=\frac{1}{1+s_{\text{scg}}}f_{\theta}^{\text{scg}}({\bm{x}}_{t})+\frac{s_{\text{scg}}}{1+s_{\text{scg}}}f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}). (8)

To enable the model to generalize across various guidance strengths, we train the model fθ​(𝒙t|α)f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}|\alpha) conditioned on a pseudo-temperature α≔1/(1+sscg)\alpha\coloneqq 1/(1+s_{\text{scg}}) from Eq. (8):

fθ​(𝒙t∣α)=α​fθscg​(𝒙t∣α)+(1−α)​sg​[fθ​(𝒙~t∣1)].f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\alpha f_{\theta}^{\text{scg}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\text{sg}[f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid 1)]. (9)

Here, α=1\alpha=1 eliminates SCG (sscg=0s_{\text{scg}}=0), while decreasing α\alpha amplifies the self-contrastive signal. Substituting Eq. (9) into standard likelihood objectives (Eqs. (1) or (2)) yields SCALE training objective. To ensure the self-generated branch fθ​(𝒙~t∣1)f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid 1) serves as a static reference for guidance, we apply a stop-gradient operator sg​[⋅]\text{sg}[\cdot] and fix α=1\alpha=1 on this branch.

We now characterize the optimal SCG prediction learned by SCALE training.

Theorem 4.1 (Optimal Solution of SCALE Training).

At an ideal regression optimum with unlimited model capacity and training data, assume the base predictor ϵθ∗(⋅∣1)\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta^{*}}(\cdot\mid 1) matches the scaled data score at the real and reference inputs. For α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1], the SCG branch satisfies

ϵθ∗scg​(𝒙t∣α)=−σt​[1α​∇𝒙t​log​pt​(𝒙t)−(1α−1)​𝔼​[∇𝒙~t​log​pt​(𝒙~t)∣𝒙t]],\bm{\epsilon}^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)\;=\;-\sigma_{t}\left[\frac{1}{\alpha}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})-\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}-1\right)\mathbb{E}\bigl[\nabla_{\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})\mid{\bm{x}}_{t}\bigr]\right], (10)

where 𝐱~t=gθ∗​(𝐱t,ϵ)\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}=g_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t},\bm{\epsilon}) is obtained by estimating the clean sample with the base predictor and re-noising it to level tt using ϵ\bm{\epsilon}. The expectation is taken over ϵ\bm{\epsilon}.

We defer the proof and an analogous result for AR models to Appendix B. Since α=1/(1+sscg)\alpha=1/(1+s_{\text{scg}}), the SCALE-trained diffusion model outputs the conditional mean SCG prediction in a single forward pass at convergence, with guidance strength controlled by α\alpha. Fig. 3 illustrates the SCALE training and sampling without external condition cc.

4.3 Practical Implementation

Regularizing SCALE via interpolation.

The analysis above assumes that 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t} and 𝒙~t\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} lie on nearby supports so that the prediction fθ​(𝒙~t)f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}) is well defined and the local density-ratio is informative. In practice, a self-generated sample can be highly degraded under limited model capacity or the stochasticity of early generation steps (t≪Tt\ll T), making direct contrast unstable [26, 25].

To address this, we regularize SCALE training by interpolating the real and self-generated samples into an intermediate support, thereby providing a stable anchor for the guidance. Concretely, we replace a fraction of patches in 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t} with those from 𝒙~t\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}. Given an interpolation ratio λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] and a per-patch Bernoulli mask Mλ∼Bernoulli⁡(λ)M_{\lambda}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\lambda), the mixed sample 𝒙~t,λ\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda} is defined as

𝒙~t,λ:=PatchMix​(𝒙t,𝒙~t,λ)=Mλ⊙𝒙~t+(1−Mλ)⊙𝒙t,\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda}:=\text{PatchMix}({\bm{x}}_{t},\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t};\lambda)=M_{\lambda}\odot\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}+(1-M_{\lambda})\odot{\bm{x}}_{t}, (11)

where ⊙\odot denotes patch-wise multiplication. This preserves local semantic structures of dense visual data and applies uniformly across both continuous and discrete data representations, unlike linear interpolation, which is ill-defined for vector-quantized tokens (see Appendix G.2). With this interpolated output, the SCG and SCALE formulations in Eq. (7) and Eq. (9) can be redefined as

fθscg​(𝒙t)=fθ​(𝒙t)+sscg​(fθ​(𝒙t)−fθ​(𝒙~t,λ)).\displaystyle f^{\text{scg}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})=f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})+s_{\text{scg}}(f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t})-f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda})). (12)
fθ​(𝒙t∣α)=α​fθscg​(𝒙t∣α)+(1−α)​sg​[fθ​(𝒙~t,λ∣1)].\displaystyle f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\alpha f_{\theta}^{\text{scg}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\text{sg}[f_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda}\mid 1)]. (13)

Reference choice and training stability.

In Eq. (13), we utilize the unguided reference from the α=1\alpha=1 slice with stop-gradient and PatchMix regularization. This stabilizes the SCALE training by keeping target dependencies acyclic and reducing the effects of reference displacement. We analyze these in the diffusion setting. (i) Unguided reference. Stop-gradient applies only to the reference branch; the same network is trained through the prediction branch with α\alpha sampled uniformly from [αmin,1][\alpha_{\min},1]. Assuming the predictor is smooth in α\alpha near 11, training at nearby values also constrains its α=1\alpha=1 slice, whose regression target is fixed by the data. The resulting chain of target definitions is acyclic within each update (data →α=1→α<1\to\alpha=1\to\alpha<1). As the α=1\alpha=1 slice converges, the SCG target stabilizes, and the α<1\alpha<1 slices can converge toward it. (ii) PatchMix. Interpolation brings the reference closer to the real input on average. For finite-capacity models, PatchMix reduces the contributions from reference displacement to the bounds on SCG target variation and prediction error by a factor of λ\sqrt{\lambda}. These bounds support using mixed samples as more reliable guidance anchors when self-generated samples are degraded. Detailed proofs are provided in Appendix C.

SCALE for conditional generation.

The basic SCALE objective sharpens sample distribution but does not enforce condition alignment, which becomes critical in large-scale visual generation. We therefore integrate CFG into SCALE training, while ensuring the inference fully guidance-free. Formally, we apply regularized SCG (Eq. 12) on top of the CFG prediction fθcfgf^{\text{cfg}}_{\theta}, which means it directly refines CFG-generated outputs using the self-contrastive signal:

fθscg-cfg​(𝒙t∣c)=fθcfg​(𝒙t∣c)+sscg​(fθcfg​(𝒙t∣c)−fθcfg​(𝒙~t,λ∣c)).\begin{split}f^{\text{{scg-cfg}}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid c)=f_{\theta}^{\text{cfg}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid c)+s_{\text{scg}}(f^{\text{cfg}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid c)-f^{\text{cfg}}_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda}\mid c)).\end{split} (14)

Following the derivation in Section 4.2, we reformulate this unified target into a learnable form:

fθcfg​(𝒙t|c,α)=α​fθscg-cfg​(𝒙t|c,α)+(1−α)​sg​[fθcfg​(𝒙~t,λ∣c,1)].\begin{split}f_{\theta}^{\text{cfg}}({\bm{x}}_{t}|c,\alpha)={\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\alpha f_{\theta}^{\text{{scg-cfg}}}({\bm{x}}_{t}|c,\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\ \text{sg}\left[f_{\theta}^{\text{cfg}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda}\mid c,1)\right]}.\end{split} (15)

Since fθcfgf_{\theta}^{\text{cfg}} on the left-hand side follows ptcfgp_{t}^{\text{cfg}}, it is not directly learnable. We therefore integrate it into the guidance-free training framework for CFG (Eq. (4)), yielding a fully tractable training target:

fθc​(𝒙t|c,α,β)=β⁡{α​fθscg-cfg​(𝒙t∣c,α,β)+(1−α)​sg​[fθcfg​(𝒙~t,λ∣c,1,β)]}+(1−β)​sg​[fθu​(𝒙t|∅,1,1)],\begin{split}&f^{c}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}|c,\alpha,\beta)=\\ &\beta\left\{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\alpha f_{\theta}^{\text{{scg-cfg}}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid c,\alpha,\beta)+(1-\alpha)\text{sg}\left[f_{\theta}^{\text{cfg}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda}\mid c,1,\beta)\right]}\right\}+(1-\beta)\ \text{sg}[f^{u}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}|\varnothing,1,1)],\end{split} (16)

where β\beta is a hyperparameter controlling the CFG scale (β=1/(1+scfg)\beta=1/(1+s_{\text{cfg}})). This formulation seamlessly integrates SCG with CFG, allowing the target trained model fθscg-cfgf_{\theta}^{\text{scg-cfg}} to be directly optimized by replacing the model prediction in Eqs. 1 and 2 with fθc​(𝒙t|c,α,β)f^{c}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}|c,\alpha,\beta). Setting β=1\beta=1 recovers basic SCALE, while setting α=1\alpha=1 reduces to the GFT [6]. Consequently, the trained model generates samples that incorporate both SCG and CFG in a single forward pass. In practice, we sample 𝒙~t\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} from the model’s unconditional prediction during training. This adds no extra cost and yields a stable reference, free from both CFG and SCG amplification. Algorithm 1 outlines the SCALE training pipeline for diffusion models. The SCALE training pipeline for AR models is in Appendix D.

4.4 Comparison with Other Methods

We compare SCALE against related methods; see Appendix F for more related works.

Computational overhead.

As summarized in Section 4.3, the training-time overhead is minimal and VRAM is unchanged relative to CFG training as the extra forward passes introduced by SCALE are computed without gradients. Since SCALE introduces minimal additional parameters for embedding α\alpha and β\beta, the parameter ratio is unchanged. We defer the detailed setup and analysis to Appendix G.1.

Versus CFG-mimicking methods.

Prior guidance-free methods train the model to reproduce the CFG distribution ptcfgp_{t}^{\text{cfg}}, so their quality is bounded by CFG itself. SCALE instead amplifies a model-based density ratio, pt​(𝒙t)/pt​(𝒙~t)p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})/p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}) for basic SCALE or ptcfg​(𝒙t|c)/ptcfg​(𝒙~t|c)p^{\text{cfg}}_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}|c)/p^{\text{cfg}}_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}|c) for CFG-augmented SCALE, providing a stronger alignment with the data distribution and superior sample quality.

Versus RL post-training.

RL post-training methods such as DPO [46] and GRPO [52] also use a contrastive signal but pursue a different goal. They align the model to human preferences via preference data or reward models and typically still rely on CFG in the visual domain [60, 38], whereas SCALE aligns to the ground-truth data distribution from the model’s own predictions and is fully guidance-free. The two are therefore complementary, and Section 5.2 shows that DPO [60] on top of SCALE further improves quality while remaining guidance-free.

5 Results

5.1 Experimental Setups

Models, datasets, and metrics.

We evaluate SCALE on class-conditional (C2I) ImageNet [9] at 256×256256\times 256 by fine-tuning DiT-XL/2 [44] and LlamaGen-L [54], and additionally train DiT-B/2 for the analysis. We report FID-50k, IS, Precision, and Recall following Dhariwal and Nichol [11]. For text-to-image generation (T2I) at 512×512512\times 512, we fine-tune Stable Diffusion v1.5 (SD1.5) [49] on LAION-Aesthetics 5+ [51] and report FID-30k, CLIP Score [45], PickScore [29], HPSv2.1 [62], Aesthetic Score [51], and Image Reward [63], complemented by a human preference study. Computational cost is measured by the number of function evaluations (NFE). See Appendix E for more details.

Baseline methods.

We compare SCALE against three groups of baselines, which enhance the base model’s performance in different ways. Guidance-free methods: We include guidance distillation [41] for diffusion models, CCA [7] for AR models, and GFT [6] for both. Guided sampling methods: We compare against CFG [20], SAG [21], and discriminator guidance (G++) [27]. For text-to-image, we further compare against RL post-training with DiffusionDPO [60]. We additionally report with representative diffusion models [11, 49, 19], and AR models [14, 66, 32, 57].

Implementation details.

We train all models with the SCALE objective in Eq. (16), introducing only a few additional hyperparameters. For fine-tuning, we limit training to less than 5%5\% of the pre-training budget and inherit the base model’s hyperparameters. We fix the PatchMix ratio at λ=0.2\lambda=0.2 across all experiments. The patch size is matched to each model’s self-attention granularity: 22 for DiT, 11 for LlamaGen, and 22 for SD1.5 (the finest self-attention resolution in its UNet). For diffusion sampling, we use 50-step DPM-Solver++ [40]. See Appendix E for the full setup.

5.2 Enhancing Guidance-free Generation with SCALE

In this section, we demonstrate that incorporating self-contrastive signal effectively enhances guidance-free generation by comparing SCALE with various generative models without guidance.

Fine-tuning from pretrained models (C2I).

We compare SCALE against baseline guidance-free methods with various generative models on class-conditional generation on ImageNet 256×256256\times 256. Among these, guidance distillation [41] applies only to diffusion models, and CCA [7] only to AR models. In contrast, SCALE and GFT apply to both. As shown in Table 2, SCALE outperforms all baselines on FID and IS across both diffusion (DiT-XL/2 [44]) and AR (LlamaGen-L [54]) models.

Fine-tuning from pretrained models (T2I).

Table 3 compares guidance-free generation results on SD1.5. The effective CFG scale for guidance-free methods is set to the standard CFG scale of 7.5. SCALE achieves superior performance while maintaining the competitive FID scores, and further improves the quality by lowering the α\alpha, confirming that the self-contrastive signal generalizes to large-scale zero-shot generation. Lowering α\alpha compensates FID but further improves the quality. The Pareto curves in Fig. 4(a), obtained by sweeping the effective CFG scale from 4.0 to 12.5 at α=0.8\alpha=0.8, show that SCALE achieves a superior CLIPScore-FID trade-off. The head-to-head comparison in Fig. 4(b) further shows SCALE winning over GFT on both HPSv2.1 and PickScore by clear margins.

SCALE vs. DPO.

As discussed in Section 4.4, SCALE and DPO operate along different perspectives. Experimental results in Fig. 4(c) demonstrate three key findings: (1) In the guidance-free setting, DPO barely improves over the SD 1.5 baseline, showing that DPO itself relies heavily on CFG for high-quality generation. (2) SCALE alone matches GFT+DPO, suggesting that self-contrastive signals are an effective alignment objective without preference data. (3) SCALE+DPO yields further gains across all metrics, indicating that the two signals are complementary rather than redundant.

The qualitative comparisons in Fig. 5 further support these findings. Without sampling-time guidance, SCALE produces samples with finer details and higher visual quality than base SD 1.5 and GFT. Applying DPO to SCALE further enhances these qualities, confirming the complementary benefits of self-contrastive signal and preference-based post-training. More qualitative comparisons of guidance-free generation with DPO post-trained models are in Figs. 11 and 12 of the Appendix.

Comparison with guided sampling.

We compare SCALE against CFG [20], information-based guidance for diffusion models (SAG [21]), and guidance that utilizes an external discriminator (G++) [27]. As shown in Table 4, while these methods introduce additional sampling overhead, SCALE matches them without any guidance at sampling, and even surpasses CFG in FID.

5.3 Analysis on SCALE

Effect of varying α\alpha and β\beta.

As noted in Section 4.3, SCALE provides inference-time flexibility for controlling the sample quality by varying α\alpha and β\beta. Fig. 6(a) visualizes their effects. Decreasing β\beta improves fidelity by amplifying the conditional signal, but stronger CFG pushes samples toward canonical templates and can change their semantic structure. Decreasing α\alpha instead targets fidelity directly while preserving semantic structure, though it may fall short when samples lie far from the data manifold (first row of Fig. 6(a)). More detailed visual analysis is provided in Appendix H.

Combination of SCG and CFG.

Aforementioned analysis suggests that SCG and CFG are complementary to each other. Therefore, we combine SCG on top of the CFG prediction, which directly rectifies the CFG-generated samples toward the data manifold. This compensates for the limitation of each individual guidance: moderate CFG enhances prompt alignment and rectifies the underlying semantic structure, while SCG improves the sample quality on top of the CFG prediction. Utilizing CFG alone with a higher guidance scale may push samples away from the data manifold or incur reduced diversity as discussed in Section 3. Notably, SCALE reduces to GFT [6] at α=1\alpha=1, which only approximates the CFG distribution. Fig. 6(b) shows that lowering α\alpha consistently improves FID and IS over this baseline. SCALE thus serves as a plug-and-play framework for improving guidance-free generation that maintains baseline performance rather than just adding complexity.

Training SCALE from scratch.

Unlike most guidance-free methods that require a CFG-trained model [41, 7], SCALE can be trained from scratch as it does not require a pretrained teacher model. Due to resource constraints, we verify this on DiT-B/2 [44], where SCALE significantly improves guidance-free generation (Table 5). Scaling to larger models is left as future work.

Interpolation type.

As discussed in Section 4.3, we employ patch-wise mix-up to maintain compatibility with diverse generative architectures. Table 6 also confirms that patch-wise mix-up provides robust improvements over linear interpolation by preserving local semantics of dense visual data.

Interpolation ratio.

Table 7 reports the impact of the interpolation ratio λ\lambda. For each λ\lambda, we report the best FID with its corresponding IS. Lower λ\lambda achieves better FID and IS, indicating that a small but non-zero λ\lambda is sufficient to provide stable and effective guidance.

6 Conclusion

We introduce SCALE, a guidance-free training framework built on self-contrastive guidance (SCG), a signal derived from the model’s own predictions on real and self-generated samples. Grounded in the information-based guidance theorem, SCG directly pushes the generation process toward the true data manifold. Extensive experiments confirm that SCALE outperforms existing guidance-free baselines on both diffusion and AR models, and show complementary performance gain when combined with human preference-based fine-tuning.

Limitations.

SCALE’s nested guidance formulation introduces additional training overhead. Extensions to broader visual alignment tasks, post-training beyond DPO, and larger, more recent generative architectures remain open directions. See Appendix I for further discussion.

Appendix A Derivation of Generalized Information-Based Guidance for Discrete Generative Models

In this section, we derive the optimization-perspective formulation of information-based guidance for discrete generative models in Eq. (6), following the framework of Tang et al. [15] and Hur et al. [24].

Let 𝒙¯t\bar{\bm{x}}_{t} denote a degraded sample that lacks some salient information hth_{t} present in the true sample 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t}, such that the data distribution decomposes as p⁡(𝒙t)=p⁡(𝒙¯t,ht)p({\bm{x}}_{t})=p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t}). Generalized information-based guidance recovers 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t} from 𝒙¯t\bar{\bm{x}}_{t} by jointly maximizing the joint likelihood and amplifying the correlation between 𝒙¯t\bar{\bm{x}}_{t} and hth_{t}, captured by p⁡(ht∣𝒙¯t)p(h_{t}\mid\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}):

arg​max𝐱¯t⁡[log⁡p⁡(𝐱¯t,ht)+s​log⁡p⁡(ht∣𝐱¯t)],\argmax_{\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}}\bigl[\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})+s\,\log p(h_{t}\mid\bar{\bm{x}}_{t})\bigr], (17)

where s≥0s\geq 0 is the guidance scale that controls the strength of information amplification.

Applying the chain rule of probability p⁡(ht∣𝒙¯t)=p⁡(𝒙¯t,ht)/p⁡(𝒙¯t)p(h_{t}\mid\bar{\bm{x}}_{t})=p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})/p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}), the conditional log-density expands as log⁡p⁡(ht∣𝒙¯t)=log⁡p⁡(𝒙¯t,ht)−log⁡p⁡(𝒙¯t)\log p(h_{t}\mid\bar{\bm{x}}_{t})=\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})-\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}). Substituting into Eq. (17) yields

arg​max𝐱¯t⁡[log⁡p⁡(𝐱¯t,ht)+s⁡(log⁡p⁡(𝐱¯t,ht)−log⁡p⁡(𝐱¯t))],\argmax_{\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}}\bigl[\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})+s\bigl(\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})-\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t})\bigr)\bigr], (18)

which recovers Eq. (6) in the main text. This formulation explicitly amplifies the pointwise mutual information log⁡p⁡(𝒙¯t,ht)−log⁡p⁡(𝒙¯t)=log⁡p⁡(ht∣𝒙¯t)\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})-\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t})=\log p(h_{t}\mid\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}) by a factor of ss on top of the base log-density log⁡p⁡(𝒙¯t|ht)=log⁡p⁡(𝒙t)\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}|h_{t})=\log p({\bm{x}}_{t}).

Connection to Hur et al. [24].

Hur et al. [24] formulate the same objective with the conditional p⁡(𝒙¯t∣ht)p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid h_{t}) in place of our joint p⁡(𝒙¯t,ht)p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t}). Since log⁡p⁡(𝒙¯t∣ht)=log⁡p⁡(𝒙¯t,ht)−log⁡p⁡(ht)\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid h_{t})=\log p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})-\log p(h_{t}) and log⁡p⁡(ht)\log p(h_{t}) does not depend on 𝒙¯t\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}, the two formulations differ only by an additive constant inside the arg​max\argmax when hth_{t} is held fixed, and therefore lead to identical optima. We adopt the joint form because it avoids treating hth_{t} as a freely defined random variable, which the conditional p⁡(𝒙¯t∣ht)p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid h_{t}) requires. Setting p⁡(𝒙¯t,ht)=p⁡(𝒙t)p(\bar{\bm{x}}_{t},h_{t})=p({\bm{x}}_{t}) instead lets us work directly with the data distribution at hand without specifying a separate distribution over hth_{t}.

Appendix B Proof of Theorem 4.1 and Analogous Result for AR Models

In this section, we derive the conditional mean SCG prediction at the diffusion regression optimum stated in Theorem 4.1, followed by the analogous result for AR models.

Proof for diffusion models.

Under the score matching objective, the optimal noise predictor ϵθ∗\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta^{*}} converges to the true scaled score from the noisy sample 𝒙t=αt​𝒙0+σt​ϵ{\bm{x}}_{t}=\alpha_{t}{\bm{x}}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\bm{\epsilon}:

ϵθ∗​(𝒙t)=−σt​∇𝒙t​log⁡pt​(𝒙t),\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t})=-\sigma_{t}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}), (19)

where tt is the diffusion timestep. Let 𝒙~t\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} be the self-generated sample from the model’s current prediction. In the context of diffusion models as a noise predictor, 𝒙~t\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} can be obtained simply. Specifically, we define a mapping gθg_{\theta} that first estimates the clean data using trained noise predictor ϵθ\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta} with Tweedie’s formula [12, 28] and subsequently re-noises it back to the same noise level tt:

𝒙~t\displaystyle\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t} =gθ​(𝒙t,ϵ)=αt​𝒙~0+σt​ϵ,where\displaystyle=g_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},\bm{\epsilon})=\alpha_{t}\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\bm{\epsilon},\,\,\text{where} (20)
𝒙~0\displaystyle\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{0} =(𝒙t−σt​ϵθ​(𝒙t))/αt,\displaystyle=({\bm{x}}_{t}-\sigma_{t}\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}))/\alpha_{t}, (21)

By the SCALE training objective, the trained model output is parameterized as the interpolation between the SCG branch and the self-generated branch:

ϵθ​(𝒙t∣α)=α​ϵθscg​(𝒙t∣α)+(1−α)​sg​[ϵθ​(𝒙~t∣1)],\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\alpha\,\bm{\epsilon}^{\text{scg}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\,\text{sg}\bigl[\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid 1)\bigr], (22)

By construction, the α=1\alpha=1 branch is the unconditional predictor,i.e., ϵθ(⋅∣1)≡ϵθ(⋅)\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid 1)\equiv\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\cdot). Hence, we may rewrite Eq. (22) as

ϵθ​(𝒙t∣α)=α​ϵθscg​(𝒙t∣α)+(1−α)​sg⁡[ϵθ​(𝒙~t)].\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\alpha\,\bm{\epsilon}^{\text{scg}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\,\operatorname{sg}\bigl[\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})\bigr]. (23)

The SCALE training directly optimizes ϵθ​(𝒙t∣α)\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha) to minimize the score matching loss

minθ⁡𝔼(𝒙0,c)∼pdata,ϵ,t​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(𝒙t∣α)‖2].\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{({\bm{x}}_{0},c)\sim p_{\text{data}},\bm{\epsilon},t}\left[||\bm{\epsilon}-\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)||^{2}\right]. (24)

The reference branch is held fixed by stop-gradient. At an ideal regression optimum (θ=θ∗\theta=\theta^{*}), the SCG branch therefore predicts the conditional mean of (ϵ−(1−α)​ϵθ∗​(𝒙~t))/α(\bm{\epsilon}-(1-\alpha)\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta^{*}}(\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}))/\alpha given 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t}. For fixed tt and α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1], using 𝔼⁡[ϵ∣𝒙t]=−σt​∇𝒙t​log⁡pt​(𝒙t)\mathbb{E}[\bm{\epsilon}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t}]=-\sigma_{t}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}) in Eq. (23) gives

α​ϵθ∗scg​(𝒙t∣α)+(1−α)​𝔼​[ϵθ∗​(𝒙~t)∣𝒙t]=−σt​∇𝒙t​log⁡pt​(𝒙t).\alpha\,\bm{\epsilon}^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta^{*}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})\mid{\bm{x}}_{t}\bigr]=-\sigma_{t}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}). (25)

Here 𝒙~t=gθ∗​(𝒙t,ϵ)\tilde{{\bm{x}}}_{t}=g_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t},\bm{\epsilon}), and the expectation is over ϵ|𝒙t\bm{\epsilon}\mid{\bm{x}}_{t}. By the assumed score accuracy at the reference inputs, ϵθ∗​(𝒙~t)=−σt​∇𝒙~t​log⁡pt​(𝒙~t)\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta^{*}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})=-\sigma_{t}\nabla_{\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}). Substituting this identity inside the expectation and solving for the SCG branch fθ∗scg​(𝒙t∣α)f^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha) gives

fθ∗scg​(𝒙t∣α)\displaystyle f^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha) =1α​[−σt​∇𝒙t​log⁡pt​(𝒙t)−(1−α)​𝔼​[ϵθ∗​(𝒙~t)∣𝒙t]]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\alpha}\Bigl[-\sigma_{t}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})-(1-\alpha)\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta^{*}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})\mid{\bm{x}}_{t}\bigr]\Bigr] (26)
=−σt​[1α​∇𝒙t​log​pt​(𝒙t)−(1α−1)​𝔼​[∇𝒙~t​log​pt​(𝒙~t)∣𝒙t]].\displaystyle=-\sigma_{t}\left[\frac{1}{\alpha}\nabla_{{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})-\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}-1\right)\mathbb{E}\bigl[\nabla_{\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})\mid{\bm{x}}_{t}\bigr]\right]. (27)

This form coincides with Eq. (10), recovering the conditional mean SCG prediction. ∎

Proof for autoregressive models.

We now derive the autoregressive (AR) counterpart, where the optimization directly works in the probability domain. For AR models, fθf_{\theta} is a next-token predictor that outputs a categorical distribution over the token vocabulary at each generation step. To match the diffusion notation, we write 𝒙t{\bm{x}}_{t} for the next-token target at position tt given 𝒙<t{\bm{x}}_{<t}.

Concretely, the next-token logit is ℓθ​(𝒙t∣α)\ell_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha) over the token vocabulary, and the predicted probability is fθ​(𝒙t∣α)=softmax⁡(ℓθ​(𝒙t∣α))f_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\mathrm{softmax}\bigl(\ell_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)\bigr). Under the cross-entropy objective in Eq. (2), the optimal next-token predictor converges to the true next-token conditional:

fθ∗​(𝒙t∣α)=pt​(𝒙t),i.e., ​ℓθ∗​(𝒙t∣α)=log⁡pt​(𝒙t)+Z⁡(α),f_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}),\qquad\text{i.e., }\ell_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})+Z(\alpha), (28)

for all α\alpha in the training distribution, where pt​(𝒙t)p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t}) refers to the true next-token distribution at position tt given 𝒙<t{\bm{x}}_{<t} and Z⁡(α)Z(\alpha) is a vocabulary-wide additive constant absorbed by the softmax normalization.

By the SCALE training objective, the trained logit is parameterized as the interpolation between the SCG branch and the self-generated branch:

ℓθ​(𝒙t∣α)=α​ℓθscg​(𝒙t∣α)+(1−α)​sg​[ℓθ​(𝒙~t∣1)],\ell_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\alpha\,\ell^{\text{scg}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\,\text{sg}\bigl[\ell_{\theta}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid 1)\bigr], (29)

where the self-generated token 𝒙~t\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} is drawn from the unconditional next-token distribution fθ(⋅∣1)f_{\theta}(\cdot\mid 1) via standard token-wise sampling. At α=1\alpha=1, the SCG branch reduces to the unconditional next-token prediction, so ℓθ∗​(𝒙~t∣1)=log⁡pt​(𝒙~t)+Z⁡(1)\ell_{\theta^{*}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}\mid 1)=\log p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})+Z(1) at convergence.

Substituting the convergence condition into the SCALE parameterization and solving for the SCG branch:

α​ℓθ∗scg​(𝒙t∣α)+(1−α)​[log⁡pt​(𝒙~t)+Z⁡(1)]=log⁡pt​(𝒙t)+Z⁡(α),\displaystyle\alpha\,\ell^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1-\alpha)\bigl[\log p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})+Z(1)\bigr]=\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})+Z(\alpha), (30)
ℓθ∗scg​(𝒙t∣α)=1α​log⁡pt​(𝒙t)−(1α−1)​log⁡pt​(𝒙~t)+Z′,\displaystyle\ell^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)=\frac{1}{\alpha}\log p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})-\Bigl(\frac{1}{\alpha}-1\Bigr)\log p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})+Z^{\prime}, (31)

where Z′Z^{\prime} denotes the sum of additive constants. With α=1/(1+sscg)\alpha=1/(1+s_{\text{scg}}), applying softmax to Eq. (31) yields

fθ∗scg​(𝒙t∣α)∝pt​(𝒙t)​[pt​(𝒙t)pt​(𝒙~t)]sscg,f^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{*}}({\bm{x}}_{t}\mid\alpha)\;\propto\;p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})\left[\frac{p_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t})}{p_{t}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t})}\right]^{s_{\text{scg}}}, (32)

which exactly matches the SCG-induced next-token distribution obtained by substituting 𝒙¯t=𝒙~t\bar{{\bm{x}}}_{t}=\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} and ht=𝒙t−𝒙~th_{t}={\bm{x}}_{t}-\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} into the discrete information-based guidance objective in Eq. (6). The SCALE-trained AR model therefore recovers the SCG distribution at convergence in the probability domain, mirroring the score-domain result for diffusion. ∎

Appendix C Analysis of the SCALE Training

The use of a self-generated reference in Eq. (9) makes the SCALE training target dependent on the model’s current predictions. We examine how this target evolves under stop-gradient updates and how prediction errors propagate through the PatchMix reference. The analysis is presented for diffusion models, where fθf_{\theta} denotes the noise predictor and ϵ\epsilon the ground-truth noise. We fix tt and α∈[αmin,1]\alpha\in[\alpha_{\min},1] with αmin>0\alpha_{\min}>0; conditional expectations average over ϵ|xt\epsilon\mid x_{t} and an independent PatchMix mask.

C.1 Training with Stop-Gradient and PatchMix

Across training iterations.

Within each update, the SCALE training target uses a frozen reference. Under stop-gradient in Eq. (9), each training step follows the target-network iteration

θk+1←θk−μ​∇θ∥ϵ−α​fθscg​(xt∣α)⏟optimization target−(1−α)​fθk​(x~t,λ∣1)⏟frozen reference(stop-gradient)∥2.\theta_{k+1}\leftarrow\theta_{k}-\mu\nabla_{\theta}\lVert\epsilon-\alpha\underbrace{f^{\text{scg}}_{\theta}(x_{t}\mid\alpha)}_{\text{optimization target}}-(1{-}\alpha)\underbrace{f_{\theta_{k}}(\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda}\mid 1)}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{frozen reference}\\ \text{(stop-gradient)}\end{subarray}}\rVert^{2}. (33)

Each iteration applies a gradient step to a regression loss with a frozen reference, evaluated at θ=θk\theta=\theta_{k}. Both x~t,λ\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda} and the prediction at that input are obtained from the α=1\alpha{=}1 slice. At α=1\alpha=1, the objective reduces to standard noise regression toward the fixed, model-independent target fθ∗(xt∣1)=−σt∇logpt(xt)f_{\theta^{\ast}}(x_{t}\mid 1)=-\sigma_{t}\nabla\log p_{t}(x_{t}). Within each update, the resulting reference dependency chain is acyclic (data →α=1→α<1\to\alpha{=}1\to\alpha{<}1); the target depends on the model but is anchored to the data distribution through the base slice’s fixed noise-regression target. Since the slices share parameters, guided-slice updates can still change the base slice across iterations.

Each gradient step.

The reference evolves across successive model snapshots (θk→θk+1\theta_{k}\to\theta_{k+1}), inducing a moving target for the α<1\alpha{<}1 slices. The target variation is bounded by the base-slice change and vanishes as this change tends to zero. Rearranging the loss in Eq. (33) gives a sample target for the SCG branch. We denote its conditional mean given xtx_{t} by T⁡[θk]T[\theta_{k}], where θk\theta_{k} specifies the fixed model snapshot used to construct and evaluate the reference:

T[θk](xt,α)=1α(−σt∇logpt(xt))−(1α−1)𝔼[fθk(x~t,λ∣1)∣xt],T[\theta_{k}](x_{t},\alpha)=\frac{1}{\alpha}\bigl(-\sigma_{t}\nabla\log p_{t}(x_{t})\bigr)-\bigl(\frac{1}{\alpha}{-}1\bigr)\mathbb{E}\bigl[f_{\theta_{k}}(\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda}\mid 1)\mid x_{t}\bigr], (34)

so a base-slice change Δf:=fθk+1(⋅∣1)−fθk(⋅∣1)\Delta f:=f_{\theta_{k+1}}(\cdot\mid 1)-f_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid 1) enters only through the last term. With a uniform change bound ∥Δ​f∥\lVert\Delta f\rVert and a common Lipschitz constant LL, we bound its effect through two contributions. First, the prediction at the reference input x~t,λ\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda} itself changes, contributing 1−αα​∥Δ​f∥\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\lVert\Delta f\rVert. Second, the base prediction also changes the generated sample x~t=xt+σt​(ϵ−fθk​(xt∣1))\tilde{x}_{t}=x_{t}+\sigma_{t}(\epsilon-f_{\theta_{k}}(x_{t}\mid 1)), shifting the reference input x~t,λ\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda}. PatchMix reduces the displacement bound from σt​∥Δ​f∥\sigma_{t}\lVert\Delta f\rVert to λ​σt​∥Δ​f∥\sqrt{\lambda}\,\sigma_{t}\lVert\Delta f\rVert in RMS. Feeding the shifted reference into the LL-Lipschitz base predictor changes its output, giving a second contribution of at most 1−αα​λ​σt​L​∥Δ​f∥\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\sqrt{\lambda}\,\sigma_{t}L\lVert\Delta f\rVert. Together,

∥Δ​T∥≤κ⁡∥Δ​f∥,κ=1−αα​(1+λ​σt​L).\lVert\Delta T\rVert\leq\kappa\,\lVert\Delta f\rVert,\qquad\kappa=\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}(1+\sqrt{\lambda}\,\sigma_{t}L). (35)

If the base slice converges uniformly to fθ∗(⋅∣1)f_{\theta^{\ast}}(\cdot\mid 1), then ∥Δ​f∥→0\lVert\Delta f\rVert\to 0 and hence ∥Δ​T∥→0\lVert\Delta T\rVert\to 0. The bound also gives T⁡[θk]→T⁡[θ∗]T[\theta_{k}]\to T[\theta^{\ast}], so the moving target settles to a fixed limit. The α<1\alpha{<}1 slices converge to it if their regression error relative to T⁡[θk]T[\theta_{k}] also vanishes.

C.2 Optimum with PatchMix under Finite Capacity Bounds

At an ideal regression optimum (θk→θ∗\theta_{k}\rightarrow\theta^{\ast}), the conditional mean of the mixed output matches the data score:

αfθ∗scg(xt∣α)+(1−α)𝔼[fθ∗(x~t,λ∣1)∣xt]=−σt∇logpt(xt).\alpha f^{\text{scg}}_{\theta^{\ast}}(x_{t}\mid\alpha)+(1{-}\alpha)\mathbb{E}\bigl[f_{\theta^{\ast}}(\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda}\mid 1)\mid x_{t}\bigr]=-\sigma_{t}\nabla\log p_{t}(x_{t}). (36)

The regression argument in the proof of Theorem 4.1 does not depend on how the reference is constructed, so it also applies under PatchMix: substituting fθ∗(x~t,λ∣1)=−σt∇logpt(x~t,λ)f_{\theta^{\ast}}(\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda}\mid 1)=-\sigma_{t}\nabla\log p_{t}(\tilde{x}_{t,\lambda}) assuming the base predictor matches the data score at the reference inputs and solving for the SCG branch gives
