Appendix D SCALE Training Pipeline for Autoregressive Models

We provide the training pipeline of SCALE for autoregressive (AR) models in Algorithm 2. The procedure mirrors the diffusion case (Algorithm 1 in the main text), with the noise predictor ϵθ\bm{\epsilon}_{\theta} replaced by the next-token predictor fθf_{\theta}, and the score-matching loss replaced by the standard cross-entropy loss on the softmax-normalized logits. PatchMix is applied at the token level along the spatial dimension following Eq. 11, and the nested guidance formulation in Eq. (16) is applied in the logit space before the softmax.

Appendix E Further Implementation Details

In this section, we provide more detailed implementation details for clarity. As denoted in the main manuscript, we explicitly follow the training recipe from the base generative models and hyperparameters [6]. For the fine-tuning, the training epoch is set to 1 5% of the pre-training. We elaborate on the detailed training configurations used for SCALE training.

Input of α,β\alpha,\beta.

Following implementation in GFT [6], we use Fourier embedding with MLP layers [49] to add conditioning for the models. For the fine-tuning, we adopt zero initialization for the conditioning network [69]. With this formulation, the additional embeddings for the α\alpha and β\beta provide a lightweight (0.0012%) parameter overhead, and negligible impact on inference latency.

PatchMix patch size.

We set the PatchMix patch size in Eq. (11) to align with the model’s self-attention granularity, so that each mixed patch respects the unit at which the model processes spatial information. For Transformer-based models with an explicit patch tokenizer, this is the token/patch size of the input: 2 for DiT-XL/2 and DiT-B/2 [44] (latent patches of size 2), and 1 for LlamaGen-L [54] (one VQ token per spatial location). For UNet-based models such as SD 1.5 [49], which contain multiple self-attention resolutions, we use the finest self-attention resolution in the latent space, corresponding to a patch size of 2.

Training and sampling.

For fine-tuning, we limit training to less than 5%5\% of the pre-training budget and inherit all hyperparameters from the base model. For training from scratch, we follow the original training recipe of the base model. For diffusion sampling, we use 50-step DPM-Solver++ [40]. For text-to-image, we additionally use LoRA [50] due to compute constraints (full setup in the SD 1.5 paragraph below). In our experiments, we found that combining CFG with SCG yields the best performance, as it provides an orthogonal guidance direction (see 5.3). To ensure that the model focuses on the effective range of guidance strengths, we set a minimum α\alpha of 0.5 for class-conditional models and 0.25 for text-to-image models during training, which corresponds to setting the maximum SCG strength as 1.0 and 3.0, respectively.

E.1 Fine-tuning

LlamaGen

We utilize LlamaGen-L for fine-tuning AR models with SCALE. We fine-tune these models with 15 epochs with a batch size of 256. The learning rate is set to 2e-4 with cosine decay. All pre-trained models are obtained from the official repository [54]. We obtain 𝒙~t\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} by categorical sampling from the unconditional logits, without temperature scaling or top-kk truncation, so that 𝒙~t\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} is drawn directly from the model’s distribution.

DiT

For the main experiments and ablation studies, we fine-tune DiT-B/2 and DiT-XL/2 with SCALE using a batch size of 256 and a learning rate of 1e-4 with cosine decay. The EMA decay rate is set to 0.9999. We observed that initializing from a pretrained from GFT objective model yields slightly better performance. We posit that incorporating self-contrastive guidance subsequent to CFG training is advantageous. For sampling, we adopt 50-step DPM-Solver++ [40].

Stable Diffusion v1.5 (Text-to-Image)

For text-to-image generation at 512×512512\times 512 resolution, we fine-tune Stable Diffusion v1.5 (SD 1.5) [49] with SCALE on LAION-Aesthetics 5+ [51], which contains 18M text-image pairs. Due to compute constraints, we use LoRA [23] with rank r=128r=128 and scaling factor 128128, trained for 50k iterations using a batch size of 256, a learning rate of 1​e−51\text{e}{-5}, and 1000 warmup steps. We initialize from a GFT fine-tuned SD 1.5 checkpoint and apply SCALE on top, which compensates for the limited capacity of LoRA. For evaluation, zero-shot FID-30k, CLIP Score [45], and Aesthetic Score [51] are measured on 30k images generated from COCO 2014 [36] validation prompts, while the human-preference metrics including PickScore [29], HPSv2.1 [62], and Image Reward [63] are measured on the Pick-a-Pic test prompts [29]. For all quantitative and qualitative results, we utilize 50-step DPM-Solver++ [40] for sampling.

DiffusionDPO on top of SCALE.

For the DPO experiment, we fine-tune the GFT and SCALE-trained SD 1.5 with DiffusionDPO [60] following the diffusers implementation33 3 github.com/huggingface/diffusers/research_projects/diffusion_dpo. We use LoRA with rank r=8r=8 and α=8\alpha=8, learning rate 1​e−51\mathrm{e}{-5}, gradient accumulation of 88 for an effective batch size of 128128, and train for 10k iterations on a single RTX 4090 GPU using the Pick-a-Pic dataset [29].

During DPO training, we fix the SCALE conditioning at α=1,β=1\alpha=1,\beta=1 (i.e., the unamplified branch) and only vary α,β\alpha,\beta at inference to control the SCG and CFG strengths. This mirrors the standard practice in language-model alignment, where DPO training is performed with sampling temperature 1.01.0 and the temperature is lowered only at inference [46, 60]. Training GFT with DPO follows the same practice, setting β=1\beta=1 for the DPO training and a lower β\beta at inference, keeping other training hyperparameters unchanged, such as LoRA rank, learning rate, and effective batch size.

E.2 Training From Scratch

Due to the computational resource limitations within an academic research setting, pre-training with large-scale visual generative models was not feasible. In this paper, to demonstrate SCALE’s applicability to pre-training, we primarily conduct experiments using DiT-B/2 models [44]. This model was selected as it requires moderate training resources, requiring 80 epochs (400k iterations with a batch size of 256) for training and taking ∼3\sim 3 days with 8 RTX4090 GPUs. For the pre-training, we drop conditions for the generated sample branch of SCALE. In this case, 𝒙¯t=𝒙~t\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}=\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} and the hth_{t} is a combination of 𝒙t−𝒙~t{\bm{x}}_{t}-\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t} and the condition cc for the information-based guidance formulation in Eqs. (5) and (6). By omitting the conditional signal, the objective initially emulates a CFG, which effectively stabilizes the model before the self-contrastive signal becomes reliable. This approach facilitates a natural curriculum, where the model first learns CFG signals and seamlessly transitions to incorporating self-contrastive signals as generation quality matures.

E.3 Human Preference Study

We complement the automated human preference metrics on SD 1.5 with a user study that directly compares SCALE against the strongest guidance-free baseline (GFT) in a side-by-side setting. The study is conducted as a blind A/B test with 20 participants, each responding to 15 image pairs for a total of 300 votes. For each trial, the participant is shown one text prompt and two generated images (A and B), one from GFT and one from SCALE, with model identities hidden and the left/right order randomized per trial. The participant is asked to select the image they prefer overall, or to choose “Tie” if the two are of comparable quality. Prompts are sampled from the Pick-a-Pic test set so that the comparison covers diverse content. An example trial is shown in Fig. 7.

Following common practice in text-to-image preference studies, participants are asked to consider three axes when making their choice:

  • •

    Text alignment: which image more accurately represents the content of the given prompt;

  • •

    Visual quality: which image exhibits better clarity, texture, and fine details;

  • •

    Photorealism: which image looks more realistic and aesthetically pleasing, without artificial artifacts.

Appendix F Related Works

F.1 Visual Generative Models

Likelihood-based visual generative models have been actively researched along several architectural lines. Diffusion models [18, 53, 43, 49, 44, 42] learn the data score and generate samples through iterative denoising. Autoregressive models [14, 54, 57, 47, 55, 34, 16, 68] factorize the joint distribution into a sequence of next-token predictions over discrete or continuous tokens. Masked generative models [4, 33, 3, 61] predict masked tokens in parallel and trade autoregressive ordering for faster sampling. Flow matching models [39, 37, 13, 31] learn a velocity field between noise and data and have recently scaled to large text-to-image systems such as Stable Diffusion 3 [13] and FLUX [31]. Despite their architectural differences, all of these families produce samples whose unconditional fidelity falls short of the training distribution and rely on additional guidance signals to close the gap.

F.2 Contrastive Signals for High-Fidelity Visual Generation

A broad range of methods enhances sample fidelity by leveraging a contrastive signal that distinguishes desired samples from undesired ones.

Information-based guidance.

Classifier-free guidance (CFG) [20] contrasts a conditional and an unconditional prediction at sampling time, amplifying the conditional signal. Information-based guidance [21, 24] generalizes CFG in terms of model-based interpretation, constructing the undesired sample from a degraded version of the input itself. From this perspective, CFG is a special case where the degradation is dropping the condition. Formally, these methods amplify any salient information hth_{t} relative to a degraded reference 𝒙¯t\bar{\bm{x}}_{t}. Self-Attention Guidance (SAG) [21] utilized a Gaussian blur to amplify high-frequency details of the input, with a self-attention mask to stabilize the guidance. Self-Guidance [24] utilizes an auxiliary model to produce a degraded reference input for the semantic vector-quantized tokens [48, 14]. While effective, these methods require additional forward passes and rely on heuristics for constructing degraded inputs, which are often domain-specific and hard to generalize to other domains.

Weak-model guidance.

These methods leverage a weaker version of the model itself to produce undesired samples. These methods generalize CFG in terms of model-based interpretation by replacing the unconditional reference with a weaker version of the model itself: autoguidance [26] contrasts the main model with a smaller or earlier checkpoint, Perturbed Attention Guidance [1] and Smoothed Energy Guidance [22] construct weak references through attention perturbation, and S2S^{2}-guidance [5] contrasts with random subnetworks of the main model, constructed by stochastic block-dropping.

Guidance-free generation.

Guidance-free methods incorporate CFG during training to enable sampling with a single model evaluation per step. Guidance distillation [41] trains a student to match the guided predictions of a pretrained diffusion teacher. Condition Contrastive Alignment (CCA) [7] fine-tunes AR models using matched and mismatched image–condition pairs and a frozen pretrained reference model, with a contrastive alignment objective whose optimum recovers the CFG sampling distribution. Guidance-Free Training (GFT) [6] retains the standard likelihood objective and reparameterizes the conditional model output as an interpolation between the sampling and unconditional predictions. This enables guidance-free training from scratch across diffusion, AR, and masked generative models. Model-guidance (MG) [56] similarly learns CFG during training, but adds a stop-gradient CFG residual directly to the regression target rather than reparameterizing the model output. These approaches derive their guidance signal from the conditional–unconditional contrast of CFG. SCALE introduces a complementary contrast between real and self-generated samples and learns it alongside CFG, aiming to improve generation beyond reproducing CFG behavior.

Reinforcement learning-based methods.

Developed from the language model alignment literature, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training methods often construct a desired and undesired contrast through reward or preference signals. Direct preference optimization (DPO) [46, 60, 71, 65, 35, 10] optimizes the policy directly on paired win–lose paired preference data. In this case, the model is to maximize the win probability over the lose probability, which implicitly encourages the model to generate samples that are preferred by the human. Recently, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [52, 38, 64, 17] samples a group of responses for each prompt and uses their reward statistics within the group as a critic-free baseline, optimizing the model with the resulting relative advantages. While effective, these methods require an external network or curated preference data and typically still rely on CFG at inference for generating high-quality samples in the visual domain.

Appendix G Additional Results

G.1 Computational Overhead Analysis

This section details the experimental setup and per-row analysis of Section 4.3 in the main text.

Measurement setup.

For diffusion models, we report the costs of fine-tuning from a pretrained checkpoint on 8×8\timesRTX 4090 GPUs. We use DiT-B/2 [44] as the base model rather than DiT-XL/2 because guidance distillation requires loading the teacher network alongside the student, and the resulting peak memory exceeds the 24 GB capacity of a single RTX 4090 at the DiT-XL/2 scale. DiT-B/2 fits comfortably for all methods and yields a fair comparison under identical hardware. For AR models, the numbers for CCA [7] and GFT are taken directly from the GFT paper [6], which measured costs on VAR-d30 [57].

Per-row analysis.

We unpack each row of Section 4.3 below.

Train time / step. The relative cost is determined by the number of model evaluations per gradient step. Guidance distillation [41] evaluates the teacher’s conditional and unconditional predictions in addition to the student’s forward pass, yielding a ×1.12\times 1.12 overhead. GFT performs only one extra unconditional forward as a stop-gradient reference, which gives the lightest overhead at ×1.06\times 1.06. SCALE matches Distillation’s ×1.12\times 1.12 because, in addition to the conditional forward, it computes a stop-gradient unconditional reference and a stop-gradient SCG reference output, both without backward passes. CCA on AR models reports a higher ×1.69\times 1.69 as it requires sampling negative tokens and an additional contrastive forward per step.

Params. SCALE introduces only the conditioning embeddings for α\alpha and β\beta (Fourier features followed by a small MLP), accounting for roughly 0.0012%0.0012\% of the base model parameters. The added parameters are therefore negligible for both model size and inference latency, leaving the parameter ratio at ×1.00\times 1.00.

VRAM. Guidance distillation must keep the teacher network resident in memory alongside the student, which inflates VRAM to ×1.21\times 1.21 on DiT-B/2 (and prevents fitting DiT-XL/2 on a 24 GB GPU). CCA similarly requires storing reference statistics for the contrastive objective, leading to ×1.39\times 1.39 on AR. GFT and SCALE, in contrast, share the same single network for all branches and only run extra forward passes without gradient retention, so VRAM remains at ×1.00\times 1.00.

Inference. All single-network guidance-free methods (Distill, CCA, GFT, SCALE) perform a single forward pass per sampling step rather than CFG’s two, halving the inference cost to ×0.50\times 0.50.

Summary.

SCALE matches GFT in memory and inference cost while keeping training-time overhead within the same order as guidance distillation, despite delivering a strictly richer training target (ptcfg​(𝒙t|c)/ptcfg​(𝒙~t|c)p_{t}^{\text{cfg}}({\bm{x}}_{t}|c)/p_{t}^{\text{cfg}}(\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t}|c) vs. ptcfg​(𝒙t|c)p_{t}^{\text{cfg}}({\bm{x}}_{t}|c)). The added cost is concentrated in two gradient-free reference passes during training and vanishes entirely at sampling time.

G.2 Visualization of PatchMix Interpolation

Fig. 8 provides additional support for the patch-wise design choice in Eq. 11. (Left) We compare linear and patch-wise interpolation in the vector-quantized (VQ) token space using the LlamaGen tokenizer [54]. For linear interpolation, we apply λ​𝒙1+(1−λ)​𝒙2\lambda{\bm{x}}_{1}+(1-\lambda){\bm{x}}_{2} on the token indices and round to the nearest integer. Despite the high structural similarity between the two source images, linear interpolation fails to preserve any semantic content at intermediate λ\lambda, since rounded VQ indices do not lie on a smooth manifold of the codebook. PatchMix, by replacing whole patches rather than interpolating coordinates, transitions smoothly from 𝒙1{\bm{x}}_{1} to 𝒙2{\bm{x}}_{2} as λ\lambda increases from 00 to 11 and remains semantically interpretable throughout. (Right) We measure the LPIPS distance [70] between 5050 real images and their PatchMix-interpolated counterparts 𝒙~t,λ\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda} on DiT-XL/2 [44], varying λ\lambda. The perceptual distance decreases monotonically as λ\lambda shrinks, confirming that a smaller λ\lambda keeps 𝒙~t,λ\tilde{\bm{x}}_{t,\lambda} close to the real-data manifold and therefore provides a stable anchor for the self-contrastive guidance.

G.3 Comparison with Guided Sampling Methods

Table 8 reports an additional comparison under the original 250-step DDPM solver of DiT-XL/2 [44], where the reported numbers for SAG [21] and G++ [27] are taken from their original papers under their original solvers, ensuring a faithful baseline. Even without any guidance at sampling time, SCALE attains the best IS and a competitive FID, surpassing CFG and remaining on par with guided sampling methods that incur substantial extra inference cost.

While SAG and G++ further improve over CFG, they do so at the price of an additional forward pass per step and rely on settings that limit their generalizability. SAG operates at a tiny guidance scale of 0.0050.005, providing only a marginal guidance signal that is unlikely to significantly improve quality over CFG. G++ adopts a timestep-aware guidance schedule tightly coupled to its solver: when transferred from the 250-step DDPM solver to the 50-step DPM-Solver++, we observe a significant degradation in IS (compared to Table 4 in the main text), indicating that its gains are sensitive to the sampling configuration. Moreover, both methods are specifically designed for score-based diffusion models and cannot be readily applied to discrete generative models such as AR models.

In contrast, SCALE delivers consistent improvements without any guidance at sampling time, achieving the highest IS in this comparison. Crucially, SCALE is agnostic to the choice of diffusion solver, applies uniformly to both diffusion and AR models, and requires no model-specific tuning, making it a broadly applicable framework for high-fidelity guidance-free generation.

Appendix H Additional Visualizations and Detailed Analysis

Fig. 9 and Fig. 10 show the samples of SCALE by varying α\alpha and β\beta using DiT-XL/2 [44] and LlamaGen-L [54], respectively. We note that all samples are generated with a single model without guidance at sampling time, and varying α\alpha and β\beta at inference time does not incur additional computational cost.

Effect of varying β\beta (implicit CFG).

By decreasing β\beta, the sample quality is improved by amplifying the conditional signal. However, it often pushes samples toward canonical templates and the semantic structure of samples can be steeply changed as CFG becomes stronger, as shown in each column of the image grid in Fig. 9 and Fig. 10. Consequently, strong CFG (i.e., lower β\beta) produces samples with reduced diversity as shown in the bottom row of each image grid.

Effect of varying α\alpha (implicit SCG).

By decreasing α\alpha, the sample quality is improved by amplifying the self-contrastive signal. It also improves the sample quality, but preserves the semantic structure as shown in each row of the image grid in Fig. 9 and Fig. 10. As a result, strong SCG (i.e., lower α\alpha) produces more diverse high-quality samples as shown in the rightmost column of each image grid. However, limitations exist. Since SCG improves the sample quality while preserving the semantic structure, it may not be able to produce high-quality samples if the unguided sample is far from the data manifold, as shown in the top row of each image grid.

Combination of SCG and CFG.

Aforementioned analysis suggests that SCG and CFG are complementary to each other. Therefore, we combine SCG on top of the CFG prediction, which directly rectifies the CFG-generated samples to the data manifold. This compensates for the limitation of each individual guidance: moderate CFG enhances prompt alignment and rectifies the underlying semantic structure, while SCG improves the sample quality on top of the CFG prediction. Utilizing CFG alone with a higher guidance scale may push samples away from the data manifold or incur reduced diversity as discussed in Section 3.

Visualization with DPO post-training.

Fig. 11 provides additional visualization of guidance-free generation with DPO post-training using stable diffusion v1.5 (SD 1.5) [49]. We note that all samples are generated with a single model without guidance at sampling time, and varying α\alpha and β\beta does not incur additional computational cost. DPO post-training without CFG at sampling time fails to produce high-quality samples. While GFT and its DPO fine-tuned model improve the sample quality, SCALE further enhances the sample quality by directly refining the samples towards the data manifold, implicitly. Fig. 12 also confirms that amplifying the SCG signal by decreasing α\alpha gradually improves the sample quality of the DPO fine-tuned SCALE model.

Appendix I Limitations and Future Work

While SCALE provides consistent gains across both class-conditional and text-to-image generation on diffusion and AR architectures, several questions remain open.

Unified guidance formulation.

The current SCALE framework is built upon the hierarchical guidance formulation, which combines the CFG and the SCG. This two-step formulation is effective by combining the benefits of each individual guidance as discussed in Appendix H, and provides an interpretable guidance signal. However, this approach inevitably introduces additional training overhead (+6%​p+6\%\text{p} per step compared to CFG). A unified, single-step guidance formulation to further improve the guidance-free training efficiency could be a promising future direction.

Extension to visual alignment tasks.

The SCALE framework currently focuses on improving the sample quality of visual generative models without guidance. However, self-contrastive signals are applicable to broader domains, such as visual alignment tasks. For instance, large visual generative models can generate unsafe, NSFW samples, which can be harmful to society. Self-contrastive signals can be used to pull the models toward the distribution of safe data while pushing it away from unsafe, NSFW distributions, without any guidance at sampling time and without loss of sample quality.

Beyond DPO post-training.

We empirically verify that SCALE is complementary to DiffusionDPO [60] by post-training a SCALE-trained model with DPO. However, our investigation is currently limited to a preliminary combination with DPO, and a systematic study of how SCALE interacts with RL-based post-training remains an open question. In particular, validating the compatibility of SCALE with more recent RL-based post-training methods, such as DSPO [71], D3PO [65], SPO [35], FlowGRPO [38], or DanceGRPO [64], would be a valuable direction for future work.

Scaling to larger and more recent generative architectures.

Our experiments cover diffusion models (DiT, SD 1.5) and AR models (LlamaGen) on academic-scale compute. Recent text-to-image models adopt rectified-flow transformers and a billion-scale parameter regime, including Stable Diffusion 3 [13] and FLUX [31]. Validating that the self-contrastive signal scales to these flow-based, large-scale models would be a promising direction.

Appendix J Ethics Statement

SCALE is a technical framework for improving the visual fidelity of guidance-free generative models. While SCALE can enhance sample quality and align outputs more closely with learned data distributions without relying on external classifier guidance, the same capabilities could be misused by unauthorized actors. Potential risks include the generation of more convincing, deceptive, or misleading visual media, with downstream harms to privacy, reputation, and public trust. Because SCALE often operates as a post-training method on pretrained backbones while sharing the training datasets, it inherits both the capabilities and the limitations of the underlying models, including any biases, memorization effects, or harmful content patterns present in their training data.

Our experiments are conducted exclusively on publicly available, well-established generative models that ship with safety filters and community-vetted usage policies. SCALE itself is not a safety mechanism; it modifies the sampling trajectory to improve fidelity but does not detect, suppress, or mitigate unsafe content. It should therefore be deployed only in conjunction with robust prompt- and output-level moderation, provenance signals (e.g., watermarking or content credentials) where appropriate, and human oversight for sensitive applications.

This work is intended for academic research and constructive applications such as creative tools, scientific visualization, and the study of guidance mechanisms in diffusion and autoregressive generative models. We explicitly prohibit malicious or unethical use, including the generation of non-consensual imagery, impersonation, disinformation, or any content intended to cause harm to individuals or groups. We encourage practitioners adopting SCALE to carefully document their assumptions and design choices, adhere to the licenses and safety settings of the underlying models, and contribute to the development of clear ethical guidelines, so as to support the responsible advancement of guidance-free generation methods and the broader generative modeling community.

Appendix K Declaration of LLM Usage

We used LLMs solely for editorial assistance. Their use was limited to polishing grammar, converting handwritten mathematical expressions into LaTeX (including the formatting of proofs in the appendix), and assisting with the visualization of figures and tables (e.g., generating boilerplate plotting code and refining layouts). The model did not contribute to ideation, research direction, or the main claims of this work, and it was not used for data analysis or core algorithmic design. All technical statements, equations, experimental results, and scientific contributions were authored and verified by the authors.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

The checklist is designed to encourage best practices for responsible machine learning research, addressing issues of reproducibility, transparency, research ethics, and societal impact. Do not remove the checklist: The papers not including the checklist will be desk rejected. The checklist should follow the references and follow the (optional) supplemental material. The checklist does NOT count towards the page limit.

Please read the checklist guidelines carefully for information on how to answer these questions. For each question in the checklist:

  • •

    You should answer [Yes] , [No] , or [N/A] .

  • •

    [N/A] means either that the question is Not Applicable for that particular paper or the relevant information is Not Available.

  • •

    Please provide a short (1–2 sentence) justification right after your answer (even for [N/A] ).

The checklist answers are an integral part of your paper submission. They are visible to the reviewers, area chairs, senior area chairs, and ethics reviewers. You will also be asked to include it (after eventual revisions) with the final version of your paper, and its final version will be published with the paper.

The reviewers of your paper will be asked to use the checklist as one of the factors in their evaluation. While [Yes] is generally preferable to [No] , it is perfectly acceptable to answer [No] provided a proper justification is given (e.g., error bars are not reported because it would be too computationally expensive” or “we were unable to find the license for the dataset we used”). In general, answering [No] or [N/A] is not grounds for rejection. While the questions are phrased in a binary way, we acknowledge that the true answer is often more nuanced, so please just use your best judgment and write a justification to elaborate. All supporting evidence can appear either in the main paper or the supplemental material, provided in appendix. If you answer [Yes] to a question, in the justification please point to the section(s) where related material for the question can be found.

IMPORTANT, please:

  • •

    Delete this instruction block, but keep the section heading “NeurIPS Paper Checklist",

  • •

    Keep the checklist subsection headings, questions/answers and guidelines below.

  • •

    Do not modify the questions and only use the provided macros for your answers.

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The claim in the abstract and introduction is comprehensively dealt with in the paper, including the background, method, results, and additional analysis in the appendix.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: The limitations are discussed in the appendix, which is also clearly stated in the conclusion of the main manuscript

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: We provide a theoretical justification of the proposed method in the main manuscript and the detailed proof in the appendix.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: We provide a detailed experimental setup for reproducing the results in the main manuscript.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [No]

  24. Justification: We do not include code for the experiments. However, the dataset and baseline code for our implementation is clearly described in the paper, which is fully publicly available.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: We provide a detailed experimental setup for training and sampling in the main manuscript. The hyperparameters for training is clearly ablated and the effect of hyperparameters for sampling is analyzed in detail.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [No]

  34. Justification: We do not include the error bars for the experiments. However, most of the reported metrics are computed over a large number of samples (50,000 for class-conditional generation and 30,000 for text-to-image generation), following the standard evaluation protocol, which is known to be statistically stable accross different runs.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: In appendix, we report the training environment, as well as required training iterations for each experiment. We also compare the computational analysis of the proposed method with the baseline methods in the main manuscript.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: We wrote a paper in compliance with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: We discuss the societal impacts of the proposed method in the appendix.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [Yes]

  54. Justification: Our work utilizes publicly released large pretrained visual generative model, Stable Diffusion 1.5 [49]. We use the model through the official diffusers library, which provides a built-in safety checker that filters NSFW and otherwise unsafe outputs by default. We do not release any large pretrained model that could be potentially misused. We only release the fine-tuning code and model weights that build upon existing checkpoints and publicly available datasets, and inherit the license and safety settings of the underlying models. While a pretrained model is involved (DiT-B/2 [44]), it poses low risk of misuse as it is relatively small and trained on publicly available, non-sensitive data (ImageNet [9]).

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  65. Guidelines:

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?
